impacts.caseName: Dental Monitoring SAS v. Align Technology, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the written description requirement from Dynamic Drinkware applies under AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(d)(2) to determine whether a reference patent is entitled to the filing date of its provisional application for prior art purposes.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's finding of obviousness and remanded, questioning the Board's reliance on its Penumbra precedent that dispensed with Dynamic Drinkware's written description analysis for AIA prior art determinations. The court scrutinized whether a reference patent can claim its provisional application's filing date as prior art without satisfying the written description requirement for the relied-upon subject matter. This decision has significant implications for how prior art dates are established in IPR proceedings under the AIA.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from a potentially narrower rule for establishing prior art dates, making it harder for IPR petitioners to use reference patents' provisional filing dates to antedate patents under review.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on IPR challenges may face greater difficulty establishing prior art status for references that claim priority to provisional applications, potentially increasing costs and uncertainty in patent validity challenges.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a trial court must defer to the terms of an existing license agreement when assessing copyright infringement damages, and what constitutes a legally permissible use of the 'book of wisdom' doctrine in calculating damages against the government.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the trial court's decision to use a hypothetical negotiation framework rather than deferring to existing license terms for copyright damages, but vacated in part because the court adopted a legally impermissible view of the book of wisdom and assessed non-compensatory damages against the government. The case involved the government's unauthorized copying of TETRA software beyond its license terms. This decision clarifies important limits on copyright damages methodology in government infringement cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software companies and copyright holders benefit from the court's affirmation that damages need not be capped at existing license rates, allowing potentially higher recovery through hypothetical negotiation frameworks.
impacts.negativeImplications: The ruling constrains how copyright holders can use post-infringement evidence (book of wisdom) to inflate damages, and limits recovery to compensatory amounts, potentially reducing awards in government infringement cases.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations in 28 U.S.C. § 2501 for claims against the government in the Court of Federal Claims is subject to American Pipe tolling.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that the six-year statute of limitations in 28 U.S.C. § 2501 is not subject to American Pipe tolling, recognizing that its prior decision in Bright v. United States was implicitly overruled by the Supreme Court's decision in California Public Employees' Retirement System v. ANZ Securities. The case involved a bank holding company that lost significant assets during the 2008 financial crisis and sued the government for breach of contract and Fifth Amendment takings. This ruling significantly limits the ability of claimants to toll limitations periods through prior class actions when suing the federal government.
impacts.positiveImplications: The government benefits from greater finality and predictability in its exposure to claims, as potential claimants cannot rely on class action filings to extend otherwise expired limitations periods.
impacts.negativeImplications: Financial institutions and investors harmed by government actions face a strict six-year deadline with no American Pipe tolling, meaning they must independently and timely file their own claims regardless of any pending class action.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly excluded trade secret damages models and whether it correctly overturned the jury's breach of contract damages award in a software licensing and trade secret misappropriation case.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's judgment on trade secret damages and remanded for a new trial, instructing the court to reconsider two previously excluded damages models. It reversed the district court's judgment on breach of contract damages and reinstated the jury award. The court also affirmed liability for trade secret misappropriation. The case arose from Ford's development of its own manufacturing configuration software after licensing Versata's software, with allegations that Ford misappropriated Versata's trade secrets in creating its replacement product.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software developers and licensors benefit from the court's reinstating the jury's breach of contract damages and requiring reconsideration of trade secret damages models, strengthening enforcement of software licensing agreements.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop internal replacements for licensed software face heightened trade secret misappropriation risk, as the court affirmed liability and expanded the scope of potentially admissible damages theories.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' in the licensed patents sufficient to constitute a virtual assignment, allowing the licensee to sue for infringement without joining the patent owner.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that the exclusive license agreement between Texas A&M University and TexasLDPC conveyed all substantial rights in the patents, entitling TexasLDPC to sue in its own name without joining A&M. The court also held that TexasLDPC had not ceased business operations merely by shifting to patent enforcement activities, so the agreement had not automatically terminated. This decision clarifies when exclusive licenses are tantamount to assignments for standing purposes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive licensees and patent assertion entities benefit from clearer standards confirming that enforcement-focused business models do not necessarily terminate license agreements, and that comprehensive exclusive licenses confer standing to sue without joining the patent owner.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose an important jurisdictional defense, as exclusive licensees with broad rights can more easily maintain infringement suits without patent owner joinder, potentially increasing patent litigation exposure.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming non-uniform constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents while affirming eligibility for claims of the '509 and '922 patents, affirmed the denial of JMOL of non-infringement, and affirmed the denial of JMOL on damages. The case involved patents related to non-uniform constellation designs used in digital communications standards (e.g., ATSC 3.0 television broadcasting). The split ruling on eligibility across related patents provides important guidance on § 101 analysis for communications technology patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies implementing communication standards benefit from the partial affirmance of eligibility and the court's endorsement of the damages model, providing certainty for standard-essential patent licensing.
impacts.negativeImplications: The vacatur of eligibility for some claims creates uncertainty for holders of patents claiming mathematical or optimization-based innovations in communications technology, potentially requiring additional proceedings to establish eligibility.

impacts.caseName: Otsuka America Pharmaceutical, Inc. v. Hetero Labs Limited
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed the claim terms 'dextromethorphan' and 'quinidine' in a pharmaceutical patent's weight-to-weight ratio limitation, and whether it permissibly waived the Rule 65(c) bond requirement pending appeal.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's claim construction and preliminary injunction preventing Hetero from launching a generic competitor to Nuedexta, a drug for treating pseudobulbar affect, but vacated the waiver of the Rule 65(c) bond requirement. The court held that the claim terms referred to the active moiety rather than salt forms of the drugs. The ruling blocks generic entry for a pharmaceutical product near patent expiration and addresses the important procedural question of bond requirements in Hatch-Waxman preliminary injunctions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Brand pharmaceutical companies benefit from the affirmance of the preliminary injunction and claim construction favoring broader patent scope, protecting market exclusivity against generic competitors near patent expiration.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic drug manufacturers face barriers to market entry, and the ruling on bond requirements means brand companies will need to post bonds pending appeal, creating financial obligations even when injunctions are upheld.

impacts.caseName: Board of Regents of the University of Texas System v. Boston Scientific Corp.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Boston Scientific was entitled to judgment as a matter of law of invalidity by anticipation and non-infringement for a patent covering drug-releasing biodegradable fiber implants used in drug-eluting coronary stents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury verdict in favor of the University of Texas, holding that Boston Scientific was entitled to JMOL of both invalidity for anticipation and non-infringement. The court overturned a damages award for UT's patent covering drug-releasing biodegradable fiber implant technology used in coronary stents. This decision eliminates a significant damages liability for Boston Scientific and narrows the scope of protection for university-held medical device patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Medical device manufacturers benefit from the reversal, which removes patent liability for drug-eluting stent technology and demonstrates that courts will rigorously evaluate anticipation defenses even after jury verdicts.
impacts.negativeImplications: University patent holders and research institutions face greater difficulty sustaining infringement verdicts in medical device cases, as appellate courts may more readily overturn jury findings on invalidity and infringement.

impacts.caseName: Range of Motion Products, LLC v. Armaid Company Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit's design patent infringement framework under Egyptian Goddess improperly focuses on differences between designs rather than overall similarity, and whether claim construction involving functionality determinations in design patents presents jury questions.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied rehearing en banc in a design patent infringement case, with significant dissenting opinions from Chief Judge Moore and others. The concurrence defended the current Egyptian Goddess framework for design patent infringement analysis, while the dissent argued the framework has been misapplied to improperly resolve infringement at summary judgment by focusing on differences rather than overall similarity. The split highlights ongoing tension in the court over design patent infringement standards.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the court's maintenance of the status quo, which permits summary judgment of non-infringement in design patent cases where differences between designs are sufficiently clear.
impacts.negativeImplications: Design patent owners face a higher bar for surviving summary judgment on infringement, as the en banc denial preserves a framework that the dissent argues improperly focuses on design differences rather than overall impression of similarity.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has appellate jurisdiction over a dispute concerning the interpretation of a patent settlement agreement phrase 'survives the EPR,' or whether this is a state law contract interpretation question within the regional circuit's jurisdiction.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked subject-matter jurisdiction over a dispute between T-Mobile and KAIFI regarding whether patent claims 'survived' an ex parte reexamination for purposes of a contingent payment obligation under a settlement agreement. The court found this was fundamentally a state law contract interpretation question, not a patent law issue, and transferred the case to the Fifth Circuit. This decision clarifies jurisdictional boundaries for post-settlement patent-related contract disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Parties to patent settlements gain clarity that contract interpretation disputes arising from settlement agreements will generally be heard in regional circuits applying state law, potentially resulting in more predictable outcomes under established contract law principles.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies involved in patent settlement disputes may face jurisdictional uncertainty and additional litigation costs as cases are transferred between circuits, and they may lose the benefit of Federal Circuit patent expertise for interpreting patent-related settlement terms.

impacts.caseName: Archroma U.S., Inc. v. Department of Commerce
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Commerce's regulation imposing a 15-day deadline for domestic interested parties to indicate intent to participate in antidumping duty sunset reviews conflicts with the governing statute.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade's invalidation of Commerce's regulation requiring domestic interested parties to indicate their intent to participate in antidumping duty sunset reviews within 15 days of initiation notice. The court held the statute was silent on the deadline and Commerce's regulatory requirement was a permissible exercise of delegated authority. This preserves Commerce's ability to efficiently administer the sunset review process for antidumping duty orders.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic manufacturers seeking to maintain antidumping protections benefit from the preservation of Commerce's structured review process, which provides clear deadlines and procedural certainty for sunset reviews.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies subject to antidumping duties may face continued trade restrictions, as the preserved 15-day participation deadline ensures domestic parties can efficiently maintain antidumping orders through sunset reviews.

impacts.caseName: VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion by dismissing a patent infringement complaint without granting leave to amend, awarding attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285, and sanctioning plaintiff's counsel under 28 U.S.C. § 1927.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal with prejudice, attorney fee award of $207,543.60 to Volkswagen, and sanctions against plaintiff's counsel in a patent infringement case involving electrically controlled spectacles. The court found VDPP had implicitly agreed not to amend its complaint in exchange for an extension, then attempted to amend anyway, and the proposed amended complaint was futile. This decision reinforces consequences for pursuing meritless patent litigation and underscores courts' willingness to impose fees and sanctions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from stronger deterrence against frivolous patent suits, as courts will award fees and impose sanctions on plaintiffs and their counsel for pursuing clearly meritless infringement claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders and their attorneys face significant financial risk from fee-shifting and sanctions if their infringement allegations are deemed baseless, potentially chilling legitimate but uncertain patent enforcement efforts.

impacts.caseName: AML IP, LLC v. Bath & Body Works Direct, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may reach the merits of a Rule 12(b)(6) patent eligibility challenge and dismiss on that ground after already concluding that venue is improper under 28 U.S.C. § 1400(b).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal of an e-commerce patent infringement case on both improper venue and patent ineligibility under § 101 grounds, even though the venue ruling alone would have been sufficient. The court held that the district court did not err by also addressing the merits of patent eligibility after finding venue improper. This ruling enables district courts to provide definitive merits rulings alongside procedural dismissals, potentially preventing repetitive litigation in different venues.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the ability of courts to resolve patent eligibility at the pleading stage alongside venue challenges, potentially achieving a merits-based dismissal that precludes re-filing in a proper venue.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face the risk that a single district court's adverse eligibility ruling on a motion to dismiss could effectively end their enforcement campaign across all jurisdictions, even when the court also dismissed for improper venue.

impacts.caseName: KG Dongbu Steel Co., Ltd. v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Court of International Trade properly sustained Commerce's determination that government-backed debt-to-equity conversions conferred no countervailable benefit to a foreign steel producer.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade and instructed it to reinstate Commerce's original determination that debt-to-equity conversions performed by Dongbu Steel conferred a countervailable subsidy. The court found that Commerce's initial equityworthiness analysis was correct and that the trial court erred by sustaining Commerce's post-remand determination (submitted under protest) finding no benefit. This decision strengthens the framework for imposing countervailing duties on imports benefiting from government-subsidized equity infusions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic steel producers and manufacturers benefit from a stronger countervailing duty framework that recognizes government-backed debt-to-equity conversions as conferring countervailable subsidies, helping level the competitive playing field against subsidized imports.
impacts.negativeImplications: Foreign manufacturers and importers face increased risk of countervailing duties when they have received government financial support through equity infusions, potentially raising costs for imported goods and disrupting international supply chains.

impacts.caseName: Exelixis, Inc. v. MSN Laboratories Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming crystalline forms of cabozantinib (L)-malate salts have adequate written description under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a), where the specification disclosed both crystalline and amorphous forms of the salt.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding that Exelixis's patents covering crystalline cabozantinib (L)-malate (the active ingredient in Cabometyx, a cancer treatment) have adequate written description, rejecting MSN's invalidity challenge. The ruling protects Exelixis's patent exclusivity for its oncology drug through 2030 against generic competition. This decision provides important guidance on written description requirements for pharmaceutical polymorphism patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical companies benefit from the affirmation that patents covering crystalline salt forms of drugs can satisfy written description requirements even when the specification also discloses amorphous forms, protecting valuable drug exclusivity.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic drug manufacturers face continued barriers to market entry for cabozantinib products, and the ruling reinforces that written description challenges to pharmaceutical polymorph patents may be difficult to sustain.
